The storm had left the path strewn with eelgrass and one lost shingle that belonged to nobody Maren knew. She walked it at first light, taking inventory the way her mother had: fence, levee, pump house, boat. All standing. The flats beyond lay rinsed and shining, as if the weather had been an apology.

Tobin came up the path with his ladder over one shoulder.

"Third rung," she said.

"I stepped over it."

"You always do."

He set the ladder against the pump house and looked out at the water, and for a while neither of them said anything, which was its own kind of conversation, one they had gotten good at over forty years.

"Chowder tonight," she said at last. "There's cream."

"There was cream in June."

"Go home, Tobin." But she said it the way she poured his cup first.
